name: MLC LLM
title: How MLC LLM Runs: Compilation, KV Cache and Tokens | Language Lineage
h1: How Does MLC LLM Turn a Compiled Model into Generated Tokens?
description: Trace MLC LLM from converted weights and TVM compilation to native runtime, prompt prefill, KV cache, sampling and token decoding on a local GPU, with primary sources.
og_subtitle: Weights + TVM library → native engine → prefill → KV cache → decode → text
verified_against: MLC LLM official compilation/deployment documentation and the published C++ model, tokenizer and sampler interfaces, fetched and read on 2026-11-12.
scope: One supported, text-only autoregressive model on one compatible local GPU. The startup toggle assumes an unchanged model, quantization, configuration and target: either missing compiled artifacts or a valid local cache. The diagram separates artifact dependencies from the logical generation loop; it is not a thread timeline or a claim that every kernel follows one universal backend. Distributed serving, speculative decoding, multimodal inputs, browser/mobile packaging, CPU execution and proprietary GPU-driver internals are out of scope.
answer: MLC LLM needs **two different artifacts**: converted model **weights** and a target-compatible **model library** containing inference logic. A first run can use **Apache TVM** to compile that library; later runs can reuse matching cached artifacts. The native runtime tokenizes the prompt, embeds its token IDs and performs **prefill** to produce next-token logits. A **sampler** selects a token. Subsequent **decode** calls process the last committed token while the **KV cache** retains earlier attention keys and values. That loop produces more tokens; detokenization converts their IDs back into text. GPU execution and Python compilation are distinct parts of the system.

sections.heading: Weights are data; the model library is executable logic
paragraphs: A weight download is not a complete executable model. MLC documents converted weights and a model library as separate inputs. The conversion command transforms or quantizes parameters; compilation specializes inference logic for the model architecture, quantization, memory-related metadata and target platform. This page follows the documented flow rather than treating a weight file as a GPU program.

The compilation documentation says converted weights can be shared across platforms. That does not make a compiled library interchangeable between targets. Its build specification includes the platform. A CUDA or Metal build and its matching configuration must be chosen for the deployment.

sections.heading: Why the first run can do more work
paragraphs: The first-run diagram includes compilation. The cached path skips that branch and reuses a matching library, but still starts the runtime and consumes model parameters. Cache reuse here assumes the same relevant artifacts and target; it is not a guarantee that changing the architecture, quantization or configuration never triggers a rebuild.

MLC describes its compiler implementation as Python code using TVM APIs. The published serving interfaces are C++. An application may expose a Python chat API while the native runtime drives compiled model functions. Compare [Transformers pipeline execution](/ai/how-transformers-runs), where Python model orchestration delegates operations to PyTorch.

sections.heading: Prefill and decode do different jobs
paragraphs: Prefill consumes prompt embeddings and returns logits for the next token. Decode consumes embeddings of the last committed token and returns logits for subsequent sampling. The model interface separately exposes a KV cache maintaining the history of processed tokens. Reusing these stored attention states is different from caching compiled code.

The feedback arrow represents repeated generation while the request remains active. It does not mean the GPU computes meaningful text directly: model functions produce logits, sampling chooses token IDs, and tokenizer decoding produces text. Exact stopping rules, sampling settings and prompt formatting depend on the request and model configuration.

sections.heading: One request is not a batching claim
paragraphs: This is a logical single-request path. MLC distinguishes synchronous MLCEngine from AsyncMLCEngine and recommends the asynchronous API for concurrent request batching. Streaming describes how output is delivered to the caller; it does not, by itself, prove how many requests the engine schedules together.

For the scheduling and cache-management layers of other serving engines, compare [vLLM](/ai/how-vllm-runs) and [SGLang](/ai/how-sglang-runs). Their architectures should not be copied onto MLC simply because all three generate tokens.

out_of_scope_note: The GPU node represents the selected compatible target, not a claim about undocumented CUDA or Metal driver internals. The diagram is a logical dependency and token-generation view.
